newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Mugabe seen missing chance on compensation demands.
newsitem.headline: Mugabe seen missing chance on compensation demands.

text.p: Zimbabwe President Robert Mugabe is missing an opportunity to end a potentially costly political controversy by refusing to acknowledge compensation demands of civilian victims of a 1980s rebellion, political analysts said.

Instead of attacking those articulating the victims' demands by accusing them of digging up skeletons to divide the southern African state, he should at least promise to look into the grievances, the analysts said.

In his first public response to a church report alleging that an army unit he deployed in the 1980s against an armed rebellion murdered 3,000 innocent civilians and committed grisly atrocities, Mugabe said the report was meant to cause trouble.

The report was submitted to Mugabe earlier this year by the Catholic Commission for Justice and Peace (CCJP). It calls on the government to acknowledge that its North Korean-trained Fifth Brigade committed "genocide" in Zimbabwe's Midlands and Matebeleland regions between 1982 and 1987 while trying to crush rebels aligned to the then main opposition ZAPU party.

It also urges the government to compensate surviving victims of the alleged atrocities, which many local political analysts say were intended to punish Ndebele people who formed the backbone of political opposition to Mugabe's rule.
The report has attracted wide publicity in the independent media and human rights groups have held seminars on the issue.
Mugabe has consistently refused to discuss the subject or acknowledge the atrocities, saying "whatever happened during the dissidents era, happened in war".
On Saturday, he said the past must be treated as such in the interest of national unity, but many political analysts believe the aggrieved and the general public will not agree.
"It was a perfect opportunity to kiss and make up and he missed it," said Lupi Mushayakarara, a leading political commentator.
"It was a denial approach and that has its limits. This is a potentially very dangerous problem...and he cannot just gloss over by talking about national unity," she told Reuters.

Speaking at the burial of an official of his ZANU-PF party on Saturday, Mugabe said of the CCJP: "These people are trying to fan factional and personal divisions among us, digging up the past so that we could end up divided on tribal and even on village lines".
The five-year rebellion ended in 1987 when Joshua Nkomo -- now one of Zimbabwe's two vice-presidents -- merged his ZAPU party with Mugabe's ZANU-PF.
But Mushayakarara believes national unity will be consolidated by acknowledging past wrongs and providing compensation.

"The longer this takes, the higher the cost politically. This is endangering the political careers of some of his closest officials," she said of top ZANU-PF officials believed to have been the forces behind the army crackdown.

John Makumbe, an outspoken political scientist at Harare's University of Zimbabwe, also said Mugabe was better off paying compensation, adding there was little support now for his 'no-apology-no-pay-approach' in his government's ranks.

Mugabe's cabinet ministers and other top ZANU-PF officials -- who normally cheer him at public functions -- looked at him in stony silence when he lashed out at his church critics over the compensation demands.
"It was a ghostly moment for many," Makumbe said.

Officials close to Mugabe -- who has ruled and dominated Zimbabwe for the last 17 years -- said the president sincerely believed the compensation issue was being used by his political opponents to undermine his position.
"That's what he says and that's the difficulty," said one official who declined to be named.
